section.heading: 3.2. The Product and Quotient Rules
section.paragraph: The formulas of this section enable us to differentiate new functions that are formed from old functions by using multiplication or division.
section.heading: The Product Rule
section.paragraph: By analogy with the Sum and Difference Rules, we might be tempted to guess, as Leibniz did three centuries ago, that the derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives. We can see, however, that this guess is wrong by looking at a particular example. Let $$f(x) = x$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2}$$ . Then the Power Rule gives $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1$$ and $$g^{\prime}(x) = 2x$$ . But $$\left( {fg} \right)(x) = x^{3}$$ , so $$\left( {fg} \right)^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2}$$ . Thus $$\left( {fg} \right)^{\prime} \neq f^{\prime}g^{\prime}$$ . The correct formula was discovered by Leibniz (soon after his false start) and is called the Product Rule.

Before stating the Product Rule, let’s see how we might discover it. We start by assuming that $$u = f(x)$$ and $$\upsilon = g(x)$$ are both positive differentiable functions. Then we can interpret the product $$u\upsilon$$ as an area of a rectangle (see Figure 1). If $$x$$ changes by an amount $$\Delta x$$ , then the corresponding changes in $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ are
$${\Delta u = f\left( {x + \Delta x} \right) - f(x) }{\Delta\upsilon = g\left( {x + \Delta x} \right) - g(x)}$$

and the new value of the product, $$\left( {u + \Delta u} \right)\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)$$ , can be interpreted as the area of the large rectangle in Figure 1 (provided that $$\Delta u$$ and $$\Delta\upsilon$$ happen to be positive).

image.alt: Details A rectangle is divided into four unequal rectangles. Among these, the horizontal rectangle at the bottom left is the larger rectangle. Its long bottom side is labeled u; the shorter side on the left is labeled v. The area inside the larger rectangle is labeled u v. The vertical rectangle at the bottom right corner has the shorter horizontal side labeled Delta u; the longer vertical side has length v. The area inside this rectangle is labeled v Delta u and is shaded. The horizontal rectangle at the top left has a shorter vertical side labeled Delta v. The area inside the rectangle is labeled u Delta v and is shaded. The area of the rectangle at the top right has length Delta u and width Delta v; its area is labeled Delta u Delta v and is shaded.

figure.caption: The geometry of the Product Rule

section.paragraph: The change in the area of the rectangle is

$$\begin{array}{lll} {\Delta\left( {u\upsilon} \right)} & = & {\left( {u + \Delta u} \right)\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right) - u\upsilon = u\Delta\upsilon + \upsilon\Delta u + \Delta u\Delta\upsilon} \\ \phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} & = & \text{the sum of the three shaded areas} \end{array}$$
If we divide by $$\Delta x$$ , we get
$$\frac{\Delta\left( {u\upsilon} \right)}{\Delta x} = u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x} + \upsilon\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} + \Delta u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}$$
If we now let $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , we get the derivative of $$u\upsilon$$ :

row.cell: $$= {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\left( {u\upsilon} \right)}{\Delta x} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\left( {u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x} + \upsilon\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} + \Delta u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}} \right)}$$

$$= {u\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x} + \upsilon\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} + \left( {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\Delta u} \right)\left( {\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}} \right)}$$

section.paragraph: Recall that in Leibniz notation the definition of a derivative can be written as
$$\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$
(Notice that $$\left. \Delta u\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ since $$f$$ is differentiable and therefore continuous.)

Although we started by assuming (for the geometric interpretation) that all the quantities are positive, we notice that Equation 1 is always true. (The algebra is valid whether $$u$$ , $$\upsilon$$ , $$\Delta u$$ , and $$\Delta\upsilon$$ are positive or negative.) So we have proved Equation 2, known as the Product Rule, for all differentiable functions $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ .

section.paragraph: In prime notation the Product Rule is written as
$$\left( {fg} \right)^{\prime} = fg^{\prime} + gf^{\prime}$$

In words, the Product Rule says that the derivative of a product of two functions is the first function times the derivative of the second function plus the second function times the derivative of the first function.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) By the Product Rule, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {xe^{ x}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {x\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) + e^{ x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {xe^{ x} + e^{ x} \cdot 1 = \left( {x + 1} \right)e^{ x}}} \end{array}$$

(b) Using the Product Rule a second time, we get $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{''}(x)} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack {\left( {x + 1} \right)e^{ x}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{f^{''}(x)} = {\left( {x + 1} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) + e^{ x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {x + 1} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{''}(x)} = {\left( {x + 1} \right)e^{ x} + e^{ x} \cdot 1 = \left( {x + 2} \right)e^{ x}}} \end{array}$$

In fact, each successive differentiation adds another term $$e^{ x}$$ , so
$$f^{(n)}(x) = \left( {x + n} \right)e^{ x}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Differentiate the function $$f(t) = \sqrt{t}\left( {a + bt} \right)$$ .
Solution 1 Using the Product Rule, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(t)} = {\sqrt{t}\frac{d}{dt}\left( {a + bt} \right) + \left( {a + bt} \right)\frac{d}{dt}\left( \sqrt{t} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\sqrt{t} \cdot b + \left( {a + bt} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{2}t^{- 1 \slash 2}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {b\sqrt{t} + \frac{a + bt}{2\sqrt{t}} = \frac{a + 3bt}{2\sqrt{t}}}} \end{array}$$
Solution 2 If we first use the laws of exponents to rewrite $$f(t)$$ , then we can proceed directly without using the Product Rule.
$$\begin{array}{rcl} {f(t)} & = & {a\sqrt{t} + bt\sqrt{t} = at^{1 \slash 2} + bt^{3 \slash 2}} \\ {f^{\prime}(t)} & = & {\frac{1}{2}at^{- 1 \slash 2} + \frac{3}{2}bt^{1 \slash 2}} \end{array}$$
which is equivalent to the answer given in Solution 1.

In Example 2, $$a$$ and $$b$$ are constants. It is customary in mathematics to use letters near the beginning of the alphabet to represent constants and letters near the end of the alphabet to represent variables.

section.paragraph: Example 2 shows that it is sometimes easier to simplify a product of functions before differentiating than to use the Product Rule. In Example 1, however, the Product Rule is the only possible method.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}g(x)$$ , where $$g(4) = 2$$ and $$g^{\prime}(4) = 3$$ , find $$f^{\prime}(4)$$ .
Solution Applying the Product Rule, we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack {\sqrt{x}g(x)} \right\rbrack = \sqrt{x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack {g(x)} \right\rbrack + g(x)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left\lbrack \sqrt{x} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\sqrt{x}g^{\prime}(x) + g(x) \cdot \frac{1}{2}x^{- 1 \slash 2}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\sqrt{x}g^{\prime}(x) + \frac{g(x)}{2\sqrt{x}}}} \end{array}$$
So
$$f^{\prime}(4) = \sqrt{4}g^{\prime}(4) + \frac{g(4)}{2\sqrt{4}} = 2 \cdot 3 + \frac{2}{2 \cdot 2} = 6.5$$

section.heading: The Quotient Rule
section.paragraph: We find a rule for differentiating the quotient of two differentiable functions $$u = f(x)$$ and $$\upsilon = g(x)$$ in much the same way that we found the Product Rule. If $$x$$ , $$u$$ , and $$\upsilon$$ change by amounts $$\Delta x$$ , $$\Delta u$$ , and $$\Delta\upsilon$$ , then the corresponding change in the quotient $$u \slash \upsilon$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\Delta\left( \frac{u}{\upsilon} \right)} = {\frac{u + \Delta u}{\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} - \frac{u}{\upsilon} = \frac{\left( {u + \Delta u} \right)\upsilon - u\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)}{\upsilon\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)}}} \\ {\phantom{\Delta\left( \frac{u}{\upsilon} \right)} = \frac{\upsilon\Delta u - u\Delta\upsilon}{\upsilon\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)}} \end{array}$$
so

$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{u}{\upsilon} \right) = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\left( {u \slash \upsilon} \right)}{\Delta x} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\upsilon\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} - u\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}}{\upsilon\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)}$$

As $$\left. \Delta x\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ , $$\left. \Delta\upsilon\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ also, because $$\upsilon = g(x)$$ is differentiable and therefore continuous. Thus, using the Limit Laws, we get

$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{u}{\upsilon} \right) = \frac{\upsilon\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x} - u\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta\upsilon}{\Delta x}}{\upsilon\lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\left( {\upsilon + \Delta\upsilon} \right)} = \frac{\upsilon\frac{du}{\mathit{dx}} - u\frac{d\upsilon}{\mathit{dx}}}{\upsilon^{2}}$$
In prime notation the Quotient Rule is written as:
$$\left( \frac{f}{g} \right)^{\prime} = \frac{gf^{\prime} - fg^{\prime}}{g^{2}}$$

In words, the Quotient Rule says that the derivative of a quotient is the denominator times the derivative of the numerator minus the numerator times the derivative of the denominator, all divided by the square of the denominator.
The Quotient Rule and the other differentiation formulas enable us to compute the derivative of any rational function, as the next example illustrates.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{l} {y^{\prime} = \frac{\left( {x^{3} + 6} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {x^{2} + x - 2} \right) - \left( {x^{2} + x - 2} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {x^{3} + 6} \right)}{\left( {x^{3} + 6} \right)^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{y^{\prime}} = \frac{\left( {x^{3} + 6} \right)\left( {2x + 1} \right) - \left( {x^{2} + x - 2} \right)\left( {3x^{2}} \right)}{\left( {x^{3} + 6} \right)^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{y^{\prime}} = \frac{\left( {2x^{4} + x^{3} + 12x + 6} \right) - \left( {3x^{4} + 3x^{3} - 6x^{2}} \right)}{\left( {x^{3} + 6} \right)^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{y^{\prime}} = \frac{- x^{4} - 2x^{3} + 6x^{2} + 12x + 6}{\left( {x^{3} + 6} \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$

Figure 3 shows the graphs of the function of Example 4 and its derivative. Notice that when $$y$$ grows rapidly (near $$- \sqrt[3]{6} \approx - 1.8$$ ), $$y^{\prime}$$ is large. And when $$y$$ grows slowly, $$y^{\prime}$$ is near $$0$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find an equation of the tangent line to the curve $$y = e^{ x} \slash \left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)$$ at the point $$\left( {1,\frac{1}{2}e} \right)$$ .
Solution According to the Quotient Rule, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) - e^{ x}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}}} = {\frac{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)e^{ x} - e^{ x}\left( {2x} \right)}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)^{2}} = \frac{e^{ x}\left( {1 - 2x + x^{2}} \right)}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}}} = \frac{e^{ x}\left( {1 - x} \right)^{2}}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)^{2}}} \end{array}$$
So the slope of the tangent line at $$\left( {1,\frac{1}{2}e} \right)$$ is
$$\left. \frac{dy}{\mathit{dx}} \right|_{x = 1} = 0$$
This means that the tangent line at $$\left( {1,\frac{1}{2}e} \right)$$ is horizontal and its equation is $$y = \frac{1}{2}e$$ . (See Figure 4.)
